extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of American constitutional law and political science; educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook-style exposition of the American federal system describing the allocation of powers, prohibitions, duties, and practical consequences of the Constitution for National and State governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: State renunciation of sovereignty on entry to Union
rubrics_metrics.description: That every State on entering the Union finally renounced its sovereignty, and is now for ever subject to the Federal authority as defined by the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a settled legal and practical principle (settled by the Civil War); frames the relationship in which States are subject to Federal authority as defined by the Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: States as satisfactory factors of the national government
rubrics_metrics.description: That the functions of the States as factors of the national government are satisfactory, i.e. sufficiently secure its strength and the dignity of these communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserts that the role delegated to States preserves both national strength and State dignity; treated as an accepted evaluative judgment rather than a point of controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delimitation of powers is convenient and needs no fundamental alteration
rubrics_metrics.description: That the delimitation of powers between the national government and the States, contained in the Constitution, is convenient, and needs no fundamental alteration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text positions this as the working consensus and foundation for subsequent descriptive discussion rather than an open debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of powers effected positively and negatively
rubrics_metrics.description: The distribution of powers between the National and the State governments is effected in two ways — Positively, by conferring certain powers on the National government; Negatively, by imposing certain restrictions on the States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the conceptual mechanism of federal allocation: explicit grants to National government and explicit prohibitions; shows why both were used (states anxious to fetter the master).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of governmental powers (five classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution divides governmental powers into: (1) Powers vested in the National government alone; (2) Powers vested in the States alone; (3) Powers exercisable by either the National government or the States; (4) Powers forbidden to the National government; (5) Powers forbidden to the State governments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This five-fold taxonomy is used throughout the chapter to organize examples and legal consequences; note that exclusivity often depends on the exercise of power rather than mere existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers vested in the National government alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Powers relating to the conduct of the foreign relations of the country and to such common national purposes as the army and navy, interstate commerce, currency, weights and measures, and the post-office, with provisions for the management of the machinery, legislative, executive, and judicial, charged with these purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given as primary examples of exclusively federal concerns; references to constitutional articles (Art. i §8, Art. ii §2, Art. iii §2, Art. iv §§3–4, Amendments xiii–xv) accompany the list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers vested in the States alone
rubrics_metrics.description: All the other ordinary powers of internal government, such as legislation on private law, civil and criminal, the maintenance of law and order, the creation of local institutions, provision for education and the relief of the poor, together with taxation for the above purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as original and inherent powers that belonged to the State before entering the Union; prima facie unlimited unless the Federal Constitution has taken them away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers exercisable concurrently by National and States
rubrics_metrics.description: Concurrent powers include legislation on some specified subjects (e.g. bankruptcy, certain commercial matters like pilot laws and harbour regulations) with State legislation giving way to Federal legislation; powers of taxation (with specific limits); certain judicial powers where Congress has not legislated; and matters related to election rules (subject to Congressional determination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains Federal preemption (State law yields in presence of Federal legislation) and specific constraints (no State may tax exports, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibitions on the National government (Art. I §9 and Bill of Rights)
rubrics_metrics.description: The National government may not suspend the writ of habeas corpus, pass a bill of attainder or an ex post facto law; give commercial preference to one State over another; grant titles of nobility; pass laws establishing or prohibiting religion or abridging freedom of speech, press, meeting, or bearing arms; require religious tests for office; try a person for a capital crime except by grand jury presentment, subject a person to double jeopardy or compel self-incrimination; or re-examine jury-determined facts except by common-law rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerated prohibitions are drawn from constitutional text and early amendments; the entry lists the most important explicit limits discussed in the chapter and notes their protective and anti-tyranny functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibitions on the States (Art. I §10 and later amendments)
rubrics_metrics.description: States shall not make treaties or alliances, coin money, make anything but gold and silver legal tender, pass bills of attainder or ex post facto laws, impair obligations of contracts, or grant titles of nobility; without Congress consent they shall not lay duties on exports or imports (with proceeds to national treasury), keep troops or ships in peacetime, enter agreements with other States or foreign powers, or engage in war unless invaded; every State must give full faith and credit to other States' records, extend privileges and immunities, deliver fugitives, and maintain a republican form of government; later amendments forbid slavery and racial disfranchisement and require due process and equal protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The long list shows how the Constitution protects the National government and individuals from State overreach; some items require Congressional consent or are qualified by later amendments (e.g. Fourteenth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance of omitted prohibitions on States
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution omits prohibitions to a State to establish or endow religion, abolish trial by jury in criminal or civil cases, suppress freedom of speech/writing/meeting (provided equally applied and not amounting to deprivation of liberty without due process), limit the electoral franchise, or extend the franchise to women, minors, or aliens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The omission is interpreted as deliberate: framers did not wish to produce uniformity among States in institutions and trusted State constitutions to protect citizens; the text emphasizes the political meaning of these absences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of a residuum of powers reserved to the people
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution leaves a residuum of powers neither granted to the Union nor continued to the States but reserved to the people; such matters can be put in force only by the difficult process of amending the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter illustrates this with the hypothetical example of California wishing to pass a measure like the Irish Land Act — such action could be barred to both State and Federal authorities without a constitutional amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption rules for State vs Federal powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Powers vested in each State are original and inherent and therefore prima facie unlimited (presumed to be enjoyed by the State unless shown to be taken away by the Federal Constitution); powers granted to the National government are delegated, enumerated and must be proved to exist (presumption is against the National government regarding unspecified powers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule of presumptions guides legal interpretation of whether a given power belongs to a State or the Federal government and is tied to the artificial/organic character of the Union vs. States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal authority is direct upon citizens, not via States
rubrics_metrics.description: The authority of the National government over the citizens of every State is direct and immediate, not exerted through the State organization, and not requiring the co-operation of the State government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Federal courts, revenue officers, post-office operate without relying on State officials; there is no local self-government in Federal matters (no Federal officials are locally elected).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited formal relations between National government and States as States
rubrics_metrics.description: The National government has little to do with the States as States; constitution requires certain services from the States (choosing senators/representatives, organizing electors, maintaining militias, keeping a republican form) but does not call upon States to contribute funds, obey administrative orders directing their authorities to carry out Federal laws, or submit their laws for Federal veto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes the framers' intent to keep the two mechanisms distinct and to minimize contact points to reduce collision; lists specific tasks the Constitution does require of States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal structure does not depend on State cooperation for continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: The National government does not allow its structure to be dependent on the action of the States; example: de facto secession of eleven States in 1860–61 did not prevent Congress from continuing to exercise its full legal powers despite diminished representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights constitutional resilience — central institutions can function despite absence or hostility of States; contrasts with federations that rely on State contributions or administrative orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal legal supremacy of State and National governments within their spheres
rubrics_metrics.description: A State is, within its proper sphere, just as legally supreme, just as well entitled to give effect to its own will, as is the National government within its sphere; both hold authority from the people and therefore one has no more right to trespass on the other's domain than vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges theoretical equality of sovereignty and addresses practical concerns about bias in Federal courts; notes that in practice unfairness has been little or none and that judicial precedent constrains departures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off between stability and executive speed in constitutional design
rubrics_metrics.description: If a nation desires perfect stability it must put up with slowness and cumbrousness; to obtain executive speed and vigour by complete concentration of power risks abuse and irrevocable steps; the American defects (waste by friction, want of unity and vigour) are the price paid for State autonomy and permanence of equilibrium among branches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framed as a normative principle for evaluating constitutional choices: protections and diffusion of power deliver permanence and security at the cost of slower action; this is advanced as an explanation for why Americans accept certain defects.
